questions.prompt: In sugar water, match each word to its part.
questions.explain: The solute dissolves in the solvent to make a solution.

questions.prompt: Sort into soluble and insoluble in water.
questions.explain: Salt, sugar and lemon juice dissolve in water; sand, chalk and sawdust do not.

questions.prompt: A solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at that temperature is…
questions.explain: A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute at that temperature.

questions.prompt: 30 g of salt is dissolved in 250 g of water. What is the mass of the solution?
20 g of sugar is dissolved in 180 g of water. What is the concentration (mass %)?
questions.hint: Divide the solute mass by the SOLUTION mass (20 + 180), then × 100.

questions.prompt: Which make sugar dissolve FASTER? Choose all that apply.
options: Using a sugar cube instead of powder
questions.explain: Stirring, heating and a larger surface area (powder) speed up dissolving. A cube has less surface area.

questions.prompt: The solubility of potassium nitrate is 32 g per 100 g water at 20 °C and 110 g at 60 °C. A saturated solution in 100 g water is cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C. What happens?
questions.hint: How much can stay dissolved at 20 °C? The rest comes out.
questions.explain: 110 − 32 = 78 g can no longer stay dissolved, so it crystallises out.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between melting and dissolving?
options: Melting involves one substance changing state; dissolving needs a solute spreading into a solvent
Dissolving needs heat but melting doesn't
questions.explain: Melting: one substance, solid → liquid. Dissolving: solute particles spread out between solvent particles.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order to measure the solubility of salt at 40 °C.
steps: Measure 100 g of water and heat it to 40 °C
Add weighed amounts of salt, stirring each time
Stop when some salt stays undissolved (saturated)
Record the total mass of salt that dissolved
questions.explain: Fix the solvent and temperature, add solute until saturated, then record.

questions.text: For most solids, solubility ___ as temperature increases. Gases are ___ soluble in warm water.
questions.explain: Most solids dissolve more when hot; gases dissolve less when hot (warm soda goes flat).

questions.prompt: A student says, 'The sugar disappeared when it dissolved, so the tea weighs the same as before.' Explain why the student is wrong, using particles.
questions.modelAnswer: The sugar didn't disappear. Its particles spread out between the water particles and became too small to see. All the sugar particles are still there, so the mass of the tea increases by the mass of the sugar added (mass is conserved).
rubric: I said the sugar particles are still there, spread out
I said they are too small to see
I said the mass increases / mass is conserved
questions.explain: Dissolving is a physical change: no particles are destroyed, so mass is conserved.
